review_note: Keep the five audiences, practical scripts, study results and protected register break. Remove self-praise, let the scripts carry the teaching, and avoid promising that partial disclosure always succeeds or costs little.

edits.before: description: "Whether to tell people, when, which people, and at what cost. Five audiences, a need without a label, a timing trap, and the one part of this course that is not a protocol."
edits.after: description: "Whether to tell people, when, which people, and at what cost. Five audiences, needs without labels, and the timing trap."
edits.reason: Describe the material a reader can use instead of advertising the forthcoming change of register.

edits.before:
the first in your family at university. The mechanics this week work for all of
them, because the evidence behind them does.
edits.after:
the first in your family at university. This week draws on research about
several concealable identities, alongside studies of autistic disclosure.
edits.reason: Describe the scope of the sources without promising that the course’s untested scripts work for every listed situation.

edits.before:
This is the week the course is most careful, and it's also the week with the
most practical scripts. Both of those are on purpose.
edits.reason: The explanations and scripts can demonstrate care without a paragraph praising their own intentions.

edits.before:
So the observers in a lab say "tell people". The people deciding whether to
tell say "it's complicated". Those aren't contradictory findings. They're
different vantage points on the same transaction, and this course won't pick
one for you.
edits.after:
A favourable first impression does not settle whether disclosure will help
someone at work. These studies ask different people, in different settings,
about different consequences.
edits.reason: Keep the distinction between study designs without putting recommendations into the participants’ mouths.

edits.before:
Everything above prices **telling**. Before the decision can be a real one,
somebody has to price the other state, because a list of reasons to be careful
is not a decision aid --- it is a thumb on one side of the scale.
edits.after: Before deciding, put **not telling** in the ledger too.
edits.reason: State the practical next step once; the following study supplies the reason for it.

edits.before:
Read the predictor carefully, because the obvious misreading is right there.
It is **not** the effort of concealing, and it is not whether you have told
anyone. It is **what you expect would happen if people knew**.
edits.after:
The predictor **anticipated stigma** is what you expect would happen if people
knew. It is not the effort of concealing, or whether you have told anyone.
edits.reason: Name the specific predictor directly instead of announcing an obvious reader mistake.

edits.before:
Two things follow.

First, two people keeping the same thing to themselves, at the same cost in
effort, are not carrying the same weight. What separates them is a belief about
the people around them.
edits.after:
Two people keeping the same thing to themselves, at the same cost in effort,
are not carrying the same weight. What separates them is a belief about the
people around them.
edits.reason: Remove a repeated course-wide signposting formula while retaining this interpretation for the separate evidence review.

edits.before:
Second, that belief is something an **environment produces**. Which means a
department where disclosure is ordinary and adjustments are unremarkable is
lowering a cost **for students who never disclose anything at all**. Hold on to
that when week 8's support staff say the fix is structural. This is the
measurement under their recommendation.
edits.after:
That belief is something an **environment produces**. Which means a department
where disclosure is ordinary and adjustments are unremarkable is lowering a
cost **for students who never disclose anything at all**.
edits.reason: Remove the closing announcement of the course’s argument; the causal interpretation itself needs a separate evidence check.

edits.before: One more structural point, and it isn't this course's invention.
edits.reason: The citation that follows already attributes the idea.

edits.before:
We read the abstract and not the paper, so we are not going to reproduce their
levels; the cut this week teaches is our own, and the next section sets it out.
What the citation earns is the shape: **disclosure has levels rather than an on
switch**, and that was described decades ago, in a different literature, about
different people. Read across to it, not straight through it --- a psychiatric
diagnosis is not an autism diagnosis and the populations are not
interchangeable. The machinery, it turns out, is largely shared.
edits.after:
We read the abstract, not the paper, so we will not reproduce their levels.
The five audiences and partial-disclosure scripts below are the course's own.
The paper gives us the idea of **levels rather than an on switch**; its
population is people with psychiatric diagnoses, not autistic students.
edits.reason: Retain the evidence boundary and population distinction without the rhetorical account of what the citation earns or the unsupported claim of shared machinery.

edits.before:
Nobody reads either one out. The show of hands is the whole result, and it is
the reason the next section exists.
edits.after: Nobody reads either sentence out. We collect only the show of hands.
edits.reason: Keep the privacy instruction; do not explain the lesson’s own structure.

edits.before:
This is the week's most useful idea: **you can disclose a need without the
label.**
edits.after: **You can disclose a need without the label.**
edits.reason: The example can establish usefulness without a superlative introduction.

edits.before:
That sentence gets the adjustment. It changes exactly one piece of what the
other person knows (Chaudoir and Fisher's third route) and nothing else. The
rest stays yours to share later, or not at all. Partial disclosure is the
course's synthesis, not a tested intervention.
edits.after:
That sentence asks for an adjustment without naming a diagnosis. It uses
Chaudoir and Fisher's third route: changing what the other person knows. You
choose whether to share the rest. Partial disclosure is the course's
synthesis, not a tested intervention.
edits.reason: A request cannot guarantee an adjustment or control every inference; keep the useful mechanism and its existing evidence limit.

edits.before: caption="Week 3's envelope, addressed on purpose. The need goes; the label is not in the envelope, and the reader has no way to tell one is missing."
edits.after: caption="Week 3's envelope. The need goes; the label stays out."
edits.reason: Let the drawing carry the metaphor without promising what its recipient can or cannot infer.

edits.before:
The way out is **low-stakes early disclosure of needs**, before anything goes
wrong: the first group meeting, the first week of a job. "Before we start: I
work best with things in writing" costs almost nothing in week 1, and a great
deal to say for the first time in week 8.
edits.after:
One option is **early disclosure of needs**: at the first group meeting or in
the first week of a job. "Before we start: I work best with things in writing."
You can make it part of the working arrangements before a problem needs
explaining.
edits.reason: Offer the existing script without claiming that early disclosure costs almost nothing for everyone.

edits.before:
Everyone in the room will be on this side of it at some point. The protocol for receiving
is short:
edits.reason: Start the receiving instructions without predicting every reader’s future.

edits.before:
The scripts above are the good case. Here is the other one, because a week that
only rehearses the good case is not preparing you for anything.

A disclosure can be received badly in three ordinary ways, and each has a
one-turn answer:
edits.after:
Here are three ways a disclosure can be received badly, with an answer you
can try:
edits.reason: Introduce the table directly and leave out praise of the course for including difficult cases.

edits.before:
None of these is a good outcome and no sentence makes it one. They are there so
that you have something to say, because the hardest part of a bad reception is
standing there with nothing.
edits.after:
These sentences cannot undo what happened. They give you something to say
without having to compose it on the spot.
edits.reason: Keep the practical limit without declaring which part of a bad reception is hardest for the reader.

edits.before:
And **anticipated stigma**, which is what you expect would happen if people
knew, and the thing the evidence says is carrying the weight.
edits.after: And **anticipated stigma** --- what you expect would happen if people knew.
edits.reason: The vocabulary recap needs the definition; the study and its four predictors have already been presented.

edits.before:
Next week, the last of the three lab sessions, and the argument this whole
course has been building towards: interoperation, not conversion.
edits.after:
Next week: interoperation, not conversion, and the last of the three
partnership lab sessions.
edits.reason: Keep the useful transition and clarify which labs are ending without announcing the course’s grand conclusion.
